title: Stocks Slip, Oil Jumps Above $88 as Renewed Mideast Strikes Revive Rate-Hike Bets — August Closes Higher
detail: US stocks fell Monday after American forces struck Iranian rocket launchers near the Strait of Hormuz — the first acknowledged US strike in the region in weeks — fueling a jump in oil prices and adding to bets the Fed will raise rates in September. Brent crude climbed roughly 2.8% back above $90/bbl intraday, while Yahoo Finance reported WTI-linked Brent futures above $88; the United States Oil Fund rose about 2.5%. The S&P 500 fell 0.33% to 7,686.14, the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 0.70% (-374.09 points) to 53,185.90, and the Nasdaq Composite slipped 0.12% to 26,370.89, ending the Dow's five-day winning streak. Higher energy costs pushed the 10-year Treasury yield toward its highest level since January 2025. Despite the pullback, all three major indexes closed out August with solid monthly gains — the S&P 500 up about 2.5%, the Nasdaq up about 3%, and the Dow up about 1.3%, marking the Dow's fifth consecutive monthly gain and the S&P/Nasdaq's first up months since May — with both the S&P 500 and Dow having touched fresh record highs earlier in the month.

title: China's August Manufacturing PMI Improves to 49.8 (Still Contracting) as G20 Finance Ministers Open Asheville Summit
detail: China's official manufacturing PMI rose to 49.8 in August, up 0.6 points from July's 49.2 and above the roughly 49.7 forecast — its second straight monthly improvement but still below the 50-point expansion threshold, extending the sector's contraction streak. The non-manufacturing PMI held flat at 49.0 (vs 49.5 expected) and the composite PMI rose to 49.5 from 49.3, with sub-indices showing production and new orders returning to expansion (50.4 and 50.6 respectively) and new export orders rebounding to 50.1 from 49.6 — a tentative sign of stabilizing external demand even as the broader economy remains soft. The same day, the G20 Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors meeting opened in Asheville, North Carolina, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Fed Chair Kevin Warsh addressing global growth. Warsh, fresh off his hawkish Jackson Hole keynote, told G20 finance leaders the world is in the midst of 'a global investment surge' reversing the prior decade's savings glut, dismissed secular-stagnation concerns, and said the Fed would have 'more work to do' absent more confidence inflation is heading to 2%. Bessent separately dismissed concerns about Treasury market health or the US national debt — which surpassed $40 trillion in August — attributing higher yields partly to stronger growth.
